# Comparative advantage and free trade (`comparative_advantage_free_trade`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/economy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Economy & finance (`economy`)
- Deps: helped by division_of_labour, positive_sum_cooperation
- Core idea: Two countries both gain from trade if each specialises in what it gives up least to produce, even if one is better at everything. Ricardo's example: Portugal needs 90 men a year for a quantity of cloth and 80 for a quantity of wine; England needs 100 and 120. At one unit of wine for one of cloth, Portugal gives up 80 worker-years to obtain cloth that would take 90 at home; England gives up 100 to obtain wine that would take 120. The everyday version: a lawyer who types faster than her clerk still gains by hiring the clerk. Lower tariffs let each country use the cheapest source, raising total income; the gains are real but not shared equally, so some producers lose.
- Pitfalls:
  - Confusing comparative with absolute advantage: 'they are better at everything, so we cannot trade' is wrong
  - Promising that everyone gains: protected producers lose and may need compensation or time to adjust
  - Judging trade by the balance of exports and imports (mercantilism) rather than by what people can consume
  - Ignoring transport costs, war and strategic dependence, and the infant-industry argument of Hamilton and List
  - Urging free trade on a city or prince whose revenue comes from tolls and customs, without offering another revenue
- History: islamic: 1838 – Treaty of Balta Liman fixes low Ottoman tariffs and abolishes monopolies, under British pressure; china: 1757–1842 – Canton system restricts foreign trade to one port; 1842 treaty ports opened by force; east_asia: 1858 – treaties impose low tariffs on Japan; europe: 1776 – Smith argues for free trade on absolute advantage; 1815 Torrens and 1817 Ricardo state comparative advantage (credit between Ricardo, Torrens and James Mill is debated); 1846 repeal of the Corn Laws; 1860 Cobden–Chevalier treaty; americas: 1791 – Hamilton's Report on Manufactures argues for protecting young industries; global: 1947 – GATT
- Read:
  - David Ricardo, On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation (1817), ch. 7
  - Douglas A. Irwin, Against the Tide: An Intellectual History of Free Trade (1996)
